Cricsheet is the current historical file source; the required runtime external API is undecided. | Basic adapter and one integration required. |\n| Worker and job queue | Process large imports, recomputation, exports, and scheduled synchronisation outside request timeouts. Jobs are idempotent, retryable, observable, and dead-lettered after bounded failures. | Intermediate. |\n| Cache | Reduce repeated reads of published statistics and reference data. Cache entries are keyed by data and definition version and invalidated after accepted corrections or recalculation. | Intermediate; introduce only after measurement. |\n| Live ingestion adapter | Receive or poll live events, order and deduplicate them, handle late corrections, and pass them through the same validation and acceptance path as file submissions. | Advanced. |\n| Custom statistic engine | Store reviewed, versioned definitions and calculate results in a restricted expression model. It must not execute arbitrary user code or unbounded database queries. | Advanced. |\n| MkDocs site | Publish architecture, API, database, security, deployment, testing, methodology, and data-source documentation independently of the product applications. | Basic; deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages. |\n\n## 5. Authorisation model\n\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\nbe preserved.\n\n| Actor | Typical permissions |\n|---|---|\n| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\n| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\n| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\n| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\n| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\n\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\n\n```text\nverified identity\nAND active application account\nAND approved-submitter capability\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\nAND route-specific permission\n```\n\nThe target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\nscope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\n`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\n`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\nstate is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor User\n    participant UI as React frontend\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n    participant API as Express API\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n    else Verified provider identity\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n        API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\n        alt Account or permission check fails\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\n        end\n    end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n  if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor Submitter\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\n    participant API as Handwritten API\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n    participant Validate as Validation service\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n    participant Files as File and export storage\n\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n    opt Raw source file retained\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n    end\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n    alt Validation fails\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n    else Valid but review required\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n    end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n   decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n   policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n   player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n  SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n  uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9. Every HTTP endpoint in this project is\r\nhand-written, so the question was whether the prohibition rules out Supabase\r\nentirely or only its generated endpoints.\r\n\r\nWritten clarification was requested from the client on 4 August 2026. The question\r\nasked whether Supabase could be used purely as a hosted PostgreSQL instance,\r\nconnected to from the team's own backend through a standard connection string,\r\nwith PostgREST never used. The client confirmed on 5 August 2026 that this is\r\nacceptable, and added that accidental use of the generated API would be penalised.\r\nThe exchange is retained with this record.\r\n\r\n## Decision\r\n\r\n**Provider.** Supabase, used solely as a managed PostgreSQL instance. The Data API\r\nwas disabled at project creation, so no generated REST or GraphQL endpoint exists\r\non the instance. The region is Central EU (Frankfurt).\r\n\r\n**Connection.** The backend connects through the Supavisor session-mode pooler on\r\nport 5432, using `DATABASE_URL` and no other configuration source. TLS is enabled\r\nand certificate verification is not disabled; the authority certificate is\r\ncommitted at `apps/backend/certs/supabase-ca.crt`.\r\n\r\n**Migrations.** `node-pg-migrate`, writing plain SQL files with explicit up and\r\ndown sections into `database/migrations`.\r\n\r\n## Alternatives considered\r\n\r\n**Direct connection instead of the pooler.** Rejected on evidence rather than\r\npreference. The direct host `db.<ref>.supabase.co` publishes no A record; a DNS\r\nquery returns only an AAAA record, and `Test-NetConnection` fails name resolution\r\nfrom a Windows client on the campus network. The direct connection therefore\r\nrequires IPv6, which cannot be assumed across six developer machines, the\r\ncontinuous integration runner and the eventual deployment target.\r\n\r\n**Transaction-mode pooler on port 6543.** Rejected because transaction mode does\r\nnot support prepared statements, which the PostgreSQL driver and most query layers\r\nrely on. The connection check probes this explicitly so that a future change of\r\nmode fails loudly rather than silently.\r\n\r\n**Drizzle Kit for migrations.** Considered and rejected. Its natural mode generates\r\nSQL from a TypeScript schema definition, which conflicts with the convention\r\nalready documented in `database/migrations/README.md` requiring ordered SQL files,\r\nand would pull the project toward an ORM that has not been chosen. It remains a\r\nreasonable option if the query-layer decision later favours it.\r\n\r\n**Other hosting providers.** Neon and Azure Database for PostgreSQL were both\r\nplausible, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL aligns with the decision to deploy on\r\nAzure. Supabase was chosen for provisioning speed and existing team familiarity,\r\nonce the compliance question had been settled in writing.\r\n\r\n## Advantages\r\n\r\n- The compliance position is settled in writing by the client, not inferred.\r\n- Disabling the Data API at creation means the prohibited endpoints do not exist,\r\n  which is a stronger guarantee than agreeing not to call them.\r\n- The connection method was selected by measurement, so it will work on every\r\n  team member's machine rather than only on those with IPv6.\r\n- Plain SQL migrations keep the schema legible and reviewable, and match the\r\n  convention the team had already documented.\r\n- No provider-specific interface is used anywhere, so changing host later requires\r\n  only a new connection string.\r\n\r\n## Disadvantages\r\n\r\n- The database is approximately 150 ms from Johannesburg. If the backend is\r\n  deployed to Azure South Africa North, that latency applies to every query.\r\n- The free plan pauses a project after a period of inactivity and retains no\r\n  backups.\r\n- The free plan's storage limit is likely to be exceeded by the agreed competition\r\n  scope. See consequence 4.\r\n- The pooler adds a component between the application and the database that can\r\n  fail independently of either.\r\n\r\n## Consequences\r\n\r\n1. The generated API must never be used. The Data API is disabled, and the team\r\n   has agreed that the Supabase client library will not be added to any workspace.\r\n2. The client's confirmation was scoped narrowly to hosted PostgreSQL over a\r\n   connection string. It does not extend to Supabase Auth, Storage, Realtime or\r\n   Edge Functions, all of which are excluded.\r\n3. Every developer needs the pooler connection string and the committed authority\r\n   certificate. Both are documented in `docs/development/setup.md`, because\r\n   neither is discoverable from the Supabase dashboard alone.\r\n4. The agreed competition scope covers eleven franchise competitions plus men's\r\n   and women's T20 internationals. The T20 international corpus alone is 1,266,835\r\n   deliveries, which is approximately 500 MB once normalised with indexes. The full\r\n   scope is likely to exceed the free plan's limit. The team must decide between\r\n   paying for additional storage, reducing scope, or moving provider, and the\r\n   decision must be recorded before ingestion begins.\r\n5. Because the plan retains no backups and all six members hold owner access on\r\n   the project, a tested dump and restore procedure is required rather than\r\n   optional.\r\n6. Schema changes are applied only through committed migrations. Using the\r\n   provider's SQL editor would leave the database out of step with the migration\r\n   history with no record of the change.\r\n\r\n## Verification and review date\r\n\r\nThe connection is verified by `npm run db:check`, which fails non-zero if the\r\ndatabase is unreachable, if certificate verification fails, or if prepared\r\nstatements are unavailable. The migration mechanism was verified by applying the\r\nbaseline migration, rolling it back, and reapplying it against the hosted\r\ndevelopment database.\r\n\r\nThis record should be reviewed when the competition scope is finalised, because\r\nconsequence 4 may force a change of provider or plan. It should be reviewed again\r\nbefore any production deployment, when the backend's Azure region is known and the\r\nlatency in the first disadvantage becomes measurable.\r\n\r\n## AI Declaration\r\n\r\nThe preceding document was planned and generated with the assistance of\r\nClaude-Web[Claude Opus 5].\r\n\n===== evidence/decisions/ADR-004-supabase-authentication-foundation.md =====\r\n# ADR-004: Supabase Authentication Foundation\r\n\r\n- **Status:** Accepted\r\n- **Date:** 2026-08-06\r\n- **Participants:** Gabriel Raz, Git Push Pray project team\r\n- **Related issues:** #14\r\n- **Related pull requests:** #24 and #34\r\n- **Supersedes:** ADR-002\r\n\r\n## Context\r\n\r\nThe Sport Analytics Tool requires managed user sign-up, sign-in, password reset and account deletion. The team may not build a custom password, session, token or OAuth implementation.\r\n\r\nThe project already uses Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL. After ADR-002 and its Firebase proof were merged, the team clarified that authentication must use Supabase Auth from the shared Supabase project.\r\n\r\nThe project must preserve separate React frontend and Express backend applications. Application data remains accessible through the team’s handwritten API rather than generated database endpoints.\r\n\r\nThis foundation must prove authenticated identity only. It must not define final application roles, approved-submitter permissions or sport-specific authorisation rules.\r\n\r\n## Decision\r\n\r\nThe project will use **Supabase Auth** as its managed authentication foundation.\r\n\r\nGoogle is enabled as the initial OAuth identity provider in the shared development Supabase project.\r\n\r\nThe intended flow is:\r\n\r\n1. The React frontend initiates a managed Google sign-in using `@supabase/supabase-js`.\r\n2. Supabase Auth completes the Google OAuth flow.\r\n3. Supabase issues an access token representing the authenticated user.\r\n4. The frontend sends the token to the handwritten Express API using the `Authorization: Bearer` header.\r\n5. The Express API validates the token using `supabase.auth.getUser(accessToken)`.\r\n6. The API uses the returned Supabase user ID as the external identity subject.\r\n\r\nThe proof-of-concept protected endpoint remains:\r\n\r\n```http\r\nGET /api/v1/auth/me\r\n```\r\n\r\nA successful response contains only the verified identity subject:\r\n\r\n```json\r\n{\r\n  \"identity\": {\r\n    \"subject\": \"<supabase-user-id>\"\r\n  }\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\nAuthentication establishes identity only. It does not grant roles, submission access or sport-specific permissions.\r\n\r\n## Account lifecycle capabilities\r\n\r\nSupabase Auth supports:\r\n\r\n- managed email/password sign-up and sign-in;\r\n- Google social sign-in;\r\n- email verification;\r\n- managed password-reset flows;\r\n- session creation, refresh and revocation;\r\n- server-side administrative user deletion.\r\n\r\nFinal account-management screens remain outside this decision.\r\n\r\nAccount deletion requires an elevated server-side administrative key and must never be performed from the browser. Its final application workflow will be designed separately.\r\n\r\n## Frontend integration\r\n\r\nThe React frontend will eventually use `@supabase/supabase-js` with:\r\n\r\n- the Supabase project URL;\r\n- a publishable key;\r\n- a configured redirect allow list;\r\n- managed session storage and refresh behaviour.\r\n\r\nThe current foundation does not implement the final sign-in interface.\r\n\r\n## Backend integration\r\n\r\nThe Express backend uses `@supabase/supabase-js` without browser session persistence.\r\n\r\nFor each protected request, the backend passes the bearer access token to:\r\n\r\n```ts\r\nsupabase.auth.getUser(accessToken);\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis performs an authenticated request to the Supabase Auth server and returns a verified user or an authentication error.\r\n\r\nThe backend does not decode an unverified token, implement custom cryptography or create a custom session system.\r\n\r\n## Environment configuration\r\n\r\nThe backend uses:\r\n\r\n```env\r\nSUPABASE_URL=https://your-project-ref.supabase.co\r\nSUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=your-supabase-publishable-key\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe frontend will use:\r\n\r\n```env\r\nVITE_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project-ref.supabase.co\r\nVITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=your-supabase-publishable-key\r\n```\r\n\r\nCommitted environment examples contain placeholders only.\r\n\r\nNo Supabase secret key, legacy `service_role` key, database password, OAuth client secret or user access token may be committed.\r\n\r\nThe Google OAuth client secret is stored only in the Google and Supabase dashboards.\r\n\r\n## Local development\r\n\r\nSupabase provides a project-scoped CLI that can run the database, Auth service and supporting tools locally.\r\n\r\nThe initial proof may use the shared hosted development project. A future local Supabase stack can be initialized and managed with the Supabase CLI in coordination with the database workstream.\r\n\r\nLocal Supabase services must not be exposed as production services.\r\n\r\n## Security consequences\r\n\r\n- Bearer access tokens are treated as secrets.\r\n- Authorization headers remain redacted from application logs.\r\n- Invalid, missing or expired tokens receive `401 Unauthorized`.\r\n- Safe error messages do not expose token-validation details.\r\n- Secret and `service_role` keys must never appear in frontend code.\r\n- Future database access must use Row Level Security or backend-enforced authorisation as appropriate.\r\n- Authentication does not automatically grant application permissions.\r\n- Final account deletion must be performed through a protected server-side workflow.\r\n\r\n## Alternatives considered\r\n\r\n### Firebase Authentication\r\n\r\nFirebase was selected in ADR-002 and successfully proved the middleware and protected-endpoint design.\r\n\r\nIt was superseded because the team requires authentication to use the existing shared Supabase platform. Retaining Firebase would introduce a second identity platform and require an additional identity-mapping boundary between Firebase and Supabase.\r\n\r\n### Auth0\r\n\r\nAuth0 provides mature OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect support, account lifecycle features and maintained React and Express integrations.\r\n\r\nIt was not selected because it would introduce an additional platform while the project already depends on Supabase and requires Supabase Auth.\r\n\r\n### Custom authentication\r\n\r\nA custom password, token or session system was rejected because it is outside the project requirements and would introduce unnecessary security risk.\r\n\r\n## Advantages\r\n\r\n- Uses an established managed authentication provider.\r\n- Aligns authentication with the existing Supabase project.\r\n- Supports Google OAuth and managed account lifecycle features.\r\n- Uses maintained frontend and backend libraries.\r\n- Preserves the handwritten Express API boundary.\r\n- Provides a stable Supabase user ID for future account mapping.\r\n- Can integrate with Row Level Security after authorisation requirements are defined.\r\n- Avoids storing or verifying passwords in application code.\r\n\r\n## Disadvantages\r\n\r\n- Couples authentication availability to Supabase.\r\n- Backend `getUser()` verification performs a network request to Supabase Auth.\r\n- Google OAuth configuration remains distributed between Google and Supabase dashboards.\r\n- Local Supabase development requires the CLI and a Docker-compatible runtime.\r\n- Account deletion requires carefully protected elevated server credentials.\r\n- Future roles and data-access policies still require separate design.\r\n\r\n## Verification\r\n\r\nThe decision is considered established when:\r\n\r\n- Google is enabled in the shared development Supabase project;\r\n- safe environment placeholders are committed;\r\n- Firebase runtime dependencies and emulator configuration are removed;\r\n- the Express backend validates a Supabase access token;\r\n- `GET /api/v1/auth/me` rejects unauthenticated requests;\r\n- the endpoint succeeds for a verified development identity;\r\n- automated tests cover missing, rejected and accepted tokens;\r\n- no credentials or user tokens are committed;\r\n- setup and architecture documentation describe the Supabase flow.\r\n\r\n## Deferred decisions\r\n\r\nThis ADR does not decide:\r\n\r\n- final roles;\r\n- approved-submitter permissions;\r\n- competition, season or fixture scope;\r\n- sport-specific authorisation;\r\n- final sign-up or sign-in screens;\r\n- final password-reset or account-deletion screens;\r\n- application profile schema;\r\n- production Row Level Security policies.\r\n\r\n## References\r\n\r\n- [Supabase Purpose and architectural principles\\n+\\n+The Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\\n+traceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\\n+from those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\\n+versioned HTTP API.\\n+\\n+The design follows these principles:\\n+\\n+1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\\n+   units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\\n+2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\\n+   consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\\n+3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\\n+   not independently entered totals.\\n+4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\\n+   approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\\n+5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\\n+6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\\n+   functionality is introduced.\\n+7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\\n+   adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\\n+\\n+## 2. Current decisions and terminology\\n+\\n+The approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\\n+agreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\\n+internationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\\n+\\n+### Authentication provider clarification\\n+\\n+Issue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\\n+was successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\\n+**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\\n+Supabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\\n+at the same time.\\n+\\n+Authentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\\n+`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\\n+the frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\\n+The provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\\n+resolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\\n+\\n+## 3. High-level architecture\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+flowchart TB\\n+    subgraph Clients[Clients]\\n+        User[Browser user]\\n+        Consumer[External API or dataset consumer]\\n+    end\\n+\\n+    subgraph Applications[Separate deployable applications]\\n+        Frontend[React and Vite frontend]\\n+        API[Handwritten Express API<br/>/api/v1]\\n+    end\\n+\\n+    Auth[Supabase Auth<br/>current managed identity provider]\\n+    External[External data or sports API<br/>adapter and source provenance]\\n+\\n+    subgraph Data[Persistent data]\\n+        DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>events, users, grants, statistics, audit)]\\n+        Files[(Object storage<br/>planned for uploads and exports)]\\n+    end\\n+\\n+    subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\\n+        Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\\n+        Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\\n+        Cache[(Cache)]\\n+        Live[Live event provider]\\n+        Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\\n+    end\\n+\\n+    User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\\n+    Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\\n+    Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\\n+    Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\\n+    Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\\n+    API -->|Verify access token| Auth\\n+    API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\\n+    API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\\n+    API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\\n+    API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\\n+    Queue -.-> Worker\\n+    Worker -.-> DB\\n+    Worker -.-> Files\\n+    API -.-> Cache\\n+    Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\\n+    Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\\n+    Definitions -.-> Worker\\n+```\\n+\\n+Solid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\\n+Intermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\\n+should store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\\n+Its provider has not yet been selected.\\n+\\n+### Trust boundaries\\n+\\n+- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\\n+- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\\n+  rules, quotas, and audit logging.\\n+- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\\n+  environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\\n+  storage credentials remain server-side.\\n+- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\\n+  privileges.\\n+- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\\n+  asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\\n+\\n+## 4. Component responsibilities\\n+\\n+| Component | Responsibility | Delivery tier and state |\\n+|---|---|---|\\n+| React frontend (`apps/frontend`) | Render responsive and accessible search, dashboard, authentication, submission, review, and export journeys. Authorisation model\\n+\\n+The minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\\n+remain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\\n+be preserved.\\n+\\n+| Actor | Typical permissions |\\n+|---|---|\\n+| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\\n+| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\\n+| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\\n+| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\\n+| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\\n+| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\\n+\\n+An approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+verified identity\\n+AND active application account\\n+AND approved-submitter capability\\n+AND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\\n+AND route-specific permission\\n+```\\n+\\n+The target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\\n+scope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\\n+`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\\n+`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\\n+state is never an authorisation control.\\n+\\n+## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+sequenceDiagram\\n+    actor User\\n+    participant UI as React frontend\\n+    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\\n+    participant API as Express API\\n+    participant DB as PostgreSQL\\n+\\n+    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\\n+    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\\n+    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\\n+    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\\n+    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\\n+    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\\n+        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\\n+    else Verified provider identity\\n+        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\\n+        API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\\n+        alt Account or permission check fails\\n+            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\\n+        else Route and resource scope allowed\\n+            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\\n+            API-->>UI: Safe response\\n+        end\\n+    end\\n+```\\n+\\n+Important controls are:\\n+\\n+- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\\n+- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\\n+- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\\n+- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\\n+- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\\n+  if supported by the selected provider;\\n+- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\\n+  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\\n+- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\\n+\\n+## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\\n+\\n+### End-to-end flow\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+sequenceDiagram\\n+    actor Submitter\\n+    participant UI as Frontend or API client\\n+    participant API as Handwritten API\\n+    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\\n+    participant Validate as Validation service\\n+    participant DB as PostgreSQL\\n+    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\\n+    participant Files as File and export storage\\n+\\n+    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\\n+    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\\n+    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\\n+    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\\n+    API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\\n+    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\\n+    opt Raw source file retained\\n+        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\\n+    end\\n+    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\\n+    alt Validation fails\\n+        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\\n+        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\\n+    else Valid but review required\\n+        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\\n+        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\\n+    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\\n+        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\\n+        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\\n+        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\\n+        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\\n+        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\\n+        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\\n+        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\\n+    end\\n+```\\n+\\n+For the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\\n+derived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\\n+creation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\\n+event cannot exist without its recalculation job.\\n+\\n+### Validation layers\\n+\\n+1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\\n+   decompression limits.\\n+2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\\n+   policy.\\n+3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\\n+   player joins.\\n+4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\\n+   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\\n+5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\\n+   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\\n+6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\\n+7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\\n+   or needs an independent reviewer.\\n+\\n+Validation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\\n+queries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\\n+accepted records or none of them.\\n+\\n+### Corrections and derivation\\n+\\n+Delivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\\n+live revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\\n+reads only the approved current-event view.\\n+\\n+Required statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\\n+the event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\\n+non-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\\n+bowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\\n+\\n+Each stored result identifies:\\n+\\n+- statistic definition and version;\\n+- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\\n+- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\\n+- calculation status and timestamp; and\\n+- value and units.\\n+\\n+A correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\\n+cache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\\n+version.\\n+\\n+## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\\n+\\n+### Uploads and source artefacts\\n+\\n+- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\\n+- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\\n+  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\\n+  SHA-256 checksums.\\n+- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\\n+  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\\n+- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\\n+  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\\n+- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\\n+  uploads are enabled.\\n+\\n+### Dataset exports\\n+\\n+Small filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\\n+return `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\\n+scope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\\n+provenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\\n+public releases may use stable public links.\\n+\\n+### External integration\\n+\\n+Cricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\\n+download and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\\n+runtime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\\n+value, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\\n+\\n+All providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\\n+submission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\\n+with jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\\n+observable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\\n+are retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\\n+not health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\\n+\\n+## 9. Basic, Intermediate, and Advanced evolution\\n+\\n+| Tier | Architecture need | Completion signal |\\n+|---|---|---|\\n+| Basic | Separate responsive frontend and handwritten versioned backend; PostgreSQL persistence; managed identity; backend roles and approved-submitter scopes; event/file submission; layered validation; traceable corrections; required derived statistics; one external integration; small exports; automated tests; CI/CD and public documentation. | A user can submit in-scope T20 events, see validation outcomes, and retrieve independently verified statistics and a documented dataset/API from deployed applications. |\\n+| Intermediate | Durable background jobs for batch ingestion, large recalculation and exports; object storage; job status and retries; caching of measured hot reads; richer review workflow; API credentials/quotas; observability, backup/restore, and performance testing. | Large real-data operations complete outside HTTP timeouts, survive retries without duplication, expose useful status, and meet agreed performance/recovery targets. |\\n+| Advanced | Live event ingestion and correction handling; versioned custom statistic definitions; dependency-aware incremental recomputation; safe expression limits; change feeds/release differences; stronger scaling and cache invalidation. | Live corrections converge on auditable results, and approved custom definitions calculate reproducibly without arbitrary code execution or unbounded resource use. |\\n+\\n+Promotion to a later tier is evidence-based. Batch processing is introduced when request-time\\n+work exceeds agreed limits; caching is introduced after profiling; live ingestion depends on a\\n+licensed reliable feed; and custom statistics depend on an approved safe definition model.\\n+\\n+## 10. Deployment and CI/CD\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+flowchart LR\\n+    Dev[Short-lived branch] --> PR[Gitea Pull Request]\\n+    PR --> CI[CI: install, structure, format,<br/>lint, typecheck, test, build]\\n+    CI --> Review[Peer review and approval]\\n+    Review --> Main[Protected main branch]\\n+    Main --> FE[Frontend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\\n+    Main --> BE[Backend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\\n+    Main --> Docs[MkDocs build and<br/>Cloudflare Pages deployment]\\n+    Migration[Reviewed SQL migrations] --> DB[(Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL)]\\n+    BE --> DB\\n+    FE --> BE\\n+    Secrets[Environment-specific secret stores] -.-> FE\\n+    Secrets -.-> BE\\n+```\\n+\\n+### Environments and deployment units\\n+\\n+- **Local:** Vite frontend on port 5173 and Express API on port 3000 run as separate\\n+  processes. Developers use safe environment placeholders and either shared development\\n+  services or an approved isolated local stack.\\n+- **Development:** the frontend and backend currently target separate Azure App Services.\\n+  PostgreSQL is hosted by Supabase in Frankfurt and reached by the backend over the TLS\\n+  Supavisor session pooler. The documentation site is deployed separately to Cloudflare\\n+  Pages.\\n+- **Preview/test:** Pull Requests always receive CI verification. Automated per-PR application\\n+  previews are desirable but not yet established.\\n+- **Production:** service names, database plan/region, storage, secrets, observability,\\n+  backups, and rollback procedures require a production decision record before release.\\n+\\n+Frontend configuration contains only browser-safe API and auth settings. Backend settings\\n+contain `DATABASE_URL`, auth verification settings, allowed origins, external API keys, and\\n+future queue/storage credentials. Gitea Action secrets or platform secret stores provide\\n+deployment credentials. Real secrets are never committed.\\n+\\n+### Pipeline controls\\n+\\n+The existing Pull Request workflow uses Node.js 20, runs `npm ci`, then `npm run check`. The\\n+repository check verifies required files, formatting, lint, TypeScript, automated tests, and\\n+all workspace builds. Before deployment is considered reliable, the pipeline must also:\\n+\\n+1. build MkDocs with `mkdocs build --strict`;\\n+2. correct the frontend/backend deployment path and workspace references so they match\\n+   `apps/frontend` and `apps/backend`;\\n+3. make deployments depend on the same green quality checks used for Pull Requests;\\n+4. run reviewed database migrations as an explicit, observable, and recoverable step rather\\n+   than on application startup;\\n+5. deploy immutable build output to the correct application;\\n+6. smoke-test frontend, API health, CORS, authentication callback, and database connectivity;\\n+7. record release identity and support rollback to the previous application version; and\\n+8. keep destructive migration changes backward-compatible across the deployment window.\\n+\\n+Path filters should deploy only affected units, while changes to contracts, root lockfiles,\\n+or shared configuration must trigger every dependent unit. Production approval gates may be\\n+added without changing application architecture.\\n+\\n+## 11. Purpose and architectural principles\n\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\nversioned HTTP API.\n\nThe design follows these principles:\n\n1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\n   units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\n2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\n   consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\n3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\n   not independently entered totals.\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\n   approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\n   functionality is introduced.\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\n   adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\n\n## 2. Current decisions and terminology\n\nThe approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\nagreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\ninternationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\n\n### Authentication provider clarification\n\nIssue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\nwas successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\n**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\nSupabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\nat the same time.\n\nAuthentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\n`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\nthe frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\nThe provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\nresolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\n\n## 3. High-level architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TB\n    subgraph Clients[Clients]\n        User[Browser user]\n        Consumer[External API or dataset consumer]\n    end\n\n    subgraph Applications[Separate deployable applications]\n        Frontend[React and Vite frontend]\n        API[Handwritten Express API<br/>/api/v1]\n    end\n\n    Auth[Supabase Auth<br/>current managed identity provider]\n    External[External data or sports API<br/>adapter and source provenance]\n\n    subgraph Data[Persistent data]\n        DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>events, users, grants, statistics, audit)]\n        Files[(Object storage<br/>planned for uploads and exports)]\n    end\n\n    subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\n        Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\n        Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\n        Cache[(Cache)]\n        Live[Live event provider]\n        Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\n    end\n\n    User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\n    Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\n    Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\n    Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\n    Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\n    API -->|Verify access token| Auth\n    API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\n    API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\n    API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\n    API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\n    Queue -.-> Worker\n    Worker -.-> DB\n    Worker -.-> Files\n    API -.-> Cache\n    Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\n    Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\n    Definitions -.-> Worker\n```\n\nSolid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\nIntermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\nshould store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\nIts provider has not yet been selected.\n\n### Trust boundaries\n\n- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\n- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\n  rules, quotas, and audit logging.\n- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\n  environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\n  storage credentials remain server-side.\n- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\n  privileges.\n- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\n  asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\n\n## 4. Component responsibilities\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Delivery tier and state |\n|---|---|---|\n| React frontend (`apps/frontend`) | Render responsive and accessible search, dashboard, authentication, submission, review, and export journeys. Perform helpful client validation and send application data only to the backend. | Basic; application scaffold exists, product journeys are planned. |\n| Express backend (`apps/backend`) | Own `/api/v1`, authoritative validation, authentication middleware, role and scope checks, event ingestion, derivation orchestration, queries, exports, external integrations, audit logs, and safe error responses. | Basic; health and identity-proof endpoints exist, domain modules are planned. |\n| Shared contracts (`packages/contracts`) | Hold versioned request/response schemas and TypeScript types shared by the applications. It contains no secrets, database access, or authorisation decisions. | Basic; health contract exists and domain contracts are planned. |\n| Supabase Auth | Manage Google OAuth and future approved account lifecycle flows; issue tokens that the backend verifies. It proves identity only. | Basic; selected and backend verification is proved. |\n| Backend authorisation | Map the verified provider subject to `app_user`, enforce account status, application role, approved-submitter state, and scoped grants on every protected route. | Basic; model and middleware are planned. |\n| PostgreSQL | Store identity mappings, grants, reference data, submissions, immutable event revisions, review and correction history, statistic definitions/results, export metadata, and audit records. Cricsheet is the current historical file source; the required runtime external API is undecided. | Basic adapter and one integration required. |\n| Worker and job queue | Process large imports, recomputation, exports, and scheduled synchronisation outside request timeouts. Jobs are idempotent, retryable, observable, and dead-lettered after bounded failures. | Intermediate. |\n| Cache | Reduce repeated reads of published statistics and reference data. Cache entries are keyed by data and definition version and invalidated after accepted corrections or recalculation. | Intermediate; introduce only after measurement. |\n| Live ingestion adapter | Receive or poll live events, order and deduplicate them, handle late corrections, and pass them through the same validation and acceptance path as file submissions. | Advanced. |\n| Custom statistic engine | Store reviewed, versioned definitions and calculate results in a restricted expression model. It must not execute arbitrary user code or unbounded database queries. | Advanced. |\n| MkDocs site | Publish architecture, API, database, security, deployment, testing, methodology, and data-source documentation independently of the product applications. | Basic; deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages. |\n\n## 5. Authorisation model\n\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\nbe preserved.\n\n| Actor | Typical permissions |\n|---|---|\n| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\n| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\n| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\n| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\n| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\n\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\n\n```text\nverified identity\nAND active application account\nAND approved-submitter capability\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\nAND route-specific permission\n```\n\nThe target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\nscope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\n`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\n`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\nstate is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor User\n    participant UI as React frontend\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n    participant API as Express API\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n    else Verified provider identity\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n        API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\n        alt Account or permission check fails\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\n        end\n    end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n  if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor Submitter\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\n    participant API as Handwritten API\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n    participant Validate as Validation service\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n    participant Files as File and export storage\n\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n    opt Raw source file retained\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n    end\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n    alt Validation fails\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n    else Valid but review required\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n    end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n   decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n   policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n   player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n  SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n  uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9.
